    Study guide

    Unit 7 · Impulse and Momentum

    How to use this: read the key ideas, then cover each worked example and try it yourself before reading the solution. Do the self-check questions on paper before you open the answers, mark the ones you miss, and come back to them in a day or two without looking. Rereading won't do much; answering questions will.

    Key ideas

    • Momentum p = mv is a vector: it points the way the object moves. A slow truck can have more momentum than a fast baseball.
    • Impulse J = FΔt is what changes momentum: J = Δp. It's the area under a force–time graph.
    • The same change in momentum can come from a big force for a short time or a small force for a long time. Airbags, padding and bending your knees all work by making Δt longer, so the force is smaller.
    • Newton's 2nd law in momentum form: ΣF = Δp/Δt. The net force is the rate at which momentum changes.
    • Bouncing beats sticking. A ball that bounces back reverses its momentum, so its Δp (and the impulse on it) is bigger than if it had stopped dead.
    • Conservation of momentum: if the net external force on a system is zero, its total momentum stays the same. In a collision the objects push each other with equal and opposite forces for the same time (3rd law), so their momentum changes cancel.
    • Collisions and explosions happen so fast that outside forces like friction and gravity barely matter during them, so momentum is conserved through the collision.
    • Elastic collision: total kinetic energy is the same before and after. Inelastic: some kinetic energy turns into thermal energy, sound and bent metal. Perfectly inelastic: the objects stick together and move off with one velocity. Momentum is conserved in all three.
    • Explosions (and recoil): starting from rest, the total momentum stays zero, so the pieces fly apart in opposite directions. Kinetic energy increases, from stored chemical or spring energy.
    • Center of mass: vcm = total momentum ÷ total mass. With no external force, the center of mass keeps the same velocity, whatever happens inside the system.
    • In 2D, conserve the x-momentum and the y-momentum separately.
    • Two-stage problems (like a ballistic pendulum): use momentum for the collision, then energy for the swing afterward. Kinetic energy is not conserved through a sticky collision.

    Equations

    p = mvmomentum (kg·m/s)
    J = FΔt = Δpimpulse (N·s), area under F–t
    ΣF = Δp/ΔtNewton's 2nd law, momentum form
    Σpbefore = Σpafterno net external force
    m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ = (m₁ + m₂)vfobjects stick together
    0 = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂explosion from rest
    vcm = (m₁v₁ + m₂v₂)/(m₁ + m₂)velocity of the center of mass
    K = ½mv² = p²/2mkinetic energy and momentum

    Common mistakes

    • Dropping the minus sign for something moving the other way. Pick a + direction and stick to it.
    • Assuming kinetic energy is conserved in every collision. Only momentum is always conserved.
    • Using conservation of energy straight through a collision where things stick.
    • Thinking the bigger object gets the bigger change in momentum. In a collision the changes are equal and opposite; the lighter object gets the bigger change in velocity.
    • Adding momenta in 2D as plain numbers. They're vectors: split them into components.
    • Mixing up impulse (N·s) and force (N). Impulse is force × time.
    • Saying a braking car's momentum “turned into heat.” Kinetic energy can become thermal energy; momentum can't. Friction hands it to the road and Earth.
    • Thinking “inelastic” means the objects stick. It only means kinetic energy was lost; sticking together is the extreme case, perfectly inelastic.
    • Giving Δp/Δt as the force asked for. It's the net force; if the question asks for one force (an airbag, the floor), take the others out using the free-body diagram.
    • Counting friction from the floor as an internal force. The floor isn't part of your system, so its friction is an outside force: it can change the system's momentum and move its center of mass even when the objects only push on each other.
    • Thinking equal and opposite forces do equal and opposite work. They act for the same time, so their impulses cancel, but the objects move different distances. In an explosion both forces do positive work, and the kinetic energy goes up.

    How to solve a collision problem

    1. Choose the system: all the objects that collide or push apart.
    2. Check that momentum is conserved: no net outside force, or the collision is so short that outside forces don't matter.
    3. Choose a + direction. Sketch before and after, with every velocity and its sign.
    4. Write Σpbefore = Σpafter (in 2D, once for x and once for y).
    5. Solve for the unknown velocity. A negative answer means it moves in the − direction.
    6. If asked about energy, compare total K before and after: equal means elastic, less means inelastic.

    Momentum or energy?

    • During a collision or explosion: momentum, always.
    • Energy too only if the collision is elastic (and the question says so).
    • Before or after the collision (sliding, swinging, falling): energy, or forces and kinematics.
    • A problem with a collision in the middle has stages. Solve them in order, and never carry kinetic energy across the collision.

    Force–time graphs

    • The area under the curve is the impulse, which equals Δp.
    • Average force = Δp ÷ contact time.
    • A longer, lower curve with the same area gives the same change in momentum with a smaller peak force.
    Impulse

    Hitting a baseball

    A 0.15 kg baseball arrives at the bat at 40 m/s and leaves at 50 m/s in the opposite direction. The bat touches it for 2.0 ms. Find the impulse on the ball and the average force from the bat.

    Take + as the way the ball leaves: vᵢ = −40 m/s and vf = +50 m/s.

    Δp=m(vf−vi)=0.15(50−(−40)) Δp=13.5N·s Favg=ΔpΔt=13.50.0020 Favg=6.8×103N

    Reversing the ball's direction is why the change is 90 m/s, not 10 m/s. The ball pushes back on the bat with the same 6.8 kN.

    Sticky collision

    A rear-end crash

    A 1200 kg car moving at 20 m/s rear-ends an 800 kg car moving the same way at 10 m/s. They lock together. How fast do they move just after? How much kinetic energy is lost?

    Momentum before = momentum after (they lock together):

    m1v1+m2v2=(m1+m2)vf (1200)(20)+(800)(10)=(2000)vf vf=16m/s

    Kinetic energy before and after:

    Ki=12(1200)(20)2+12(800)(10)2=280kJ Kf=12(2000)(16)2=256kJ ΔK=−24kJ (lost)

    Momentum is conserved exactly, but kinetic energy isn't: the 24 kJ went into crumpling metal, sound and heating.

    Explosion

    Two carts pushed apart by a spring

    A 2.0 kg cart and a 0.50 kg cart are held together at rest with a squashed spring between them. When released, the light cart moves off at 4.0 m/s. How fast does the heavy cart move? How much energy did the spring store?

    The total momentum starts at zero and stays zero:

    0=m1v1+m2v2=(0.50)(4.0)+(2.0)v v=−1.0m/s (the opposite way)

    The spring's energy becomes the carts' kinetic energy:

    Us=12(0.50)(4.0)2+12(2.0)(1.0)2 Us=5.0J

    The momenta are equal and opposite (2.0 kg·m/s each), but the light cart gets 4 J of the 5 J. In an explosion the lighter piece always carries off most of the kinetic energy.

    Two stages

    A ballistic pendulum

    A 0.050 kg clay ball hits a 0.95 kg block hanging on a string and sticks. The block and clay swing up 0.20 m. How fast was the clay moving?

    Stage 2 (the swing, energy) gives the speed just after the hit:

    12v2=gh →v=2gh=2(10)(0.20)=2.0m/s

    Stage 1 (the collision, momentum):

    mclayvclay=(mclay+mblock)v (0.050)vclay=(1.0)(2.0) vclay=40m/s

    Work backward: the swing tells you the speed just after the hit. The clay starts with 40 J of kinetic energy and the swing only has 2 J, so 95% of it was lost in the sticky collision. That's why energy can't be used across it.

    Collision in 2D

    Two cars at an intersection

    A 1000 kg car heading east at 20 m/s collides with a 1500 kg car heading north at 10 m/s. They stick together. Find their speed and direction just after.

    Conserve each direction separately:

    px=(1000)(20)=20000kg·m/s py=(1500)(10)=15000kg·m/s p=px2+py2=200002+150002=25000kg·m/s v=pmtotal=250002500 v=10m/s θ=tan−1(1500020000)=37∘ north of east

    Each direction keeps its own momentum. The wreck heads mostly east because the east-moving car brought more momentum.

    More examples

    Click an example to open it.

    Impulse, then one force

    An airbag and a seatbelt

    In a crash test, a 60 kg dummy moving forward at 15 m/s is brought to rest in 0.12 s by the seatbelt and the airbag pushing on it together. The seatbelt's average force on the dummy is 4500 N. What is the airbag's average force on it?

    System: the dummy. Take + as forward. The impulse–momentum theorem gives the net force:

    Fnet=ΔpΔt=(60)(0−15)0.12 Fnet=−7500N (backward)

    That is the total of both pushes, which both point backward. The weight and the seat's upward push are vertical and cancel, so they don't enter:

    Fbelt+Fbag=7500N Fbag=7500−4500 Fbag=3000N backward

    Δp/Δt gives the net force, not the force from any one object; 7500 N is not the answer. Find the net force first, then split it up with the free-body diagram. When the motion is vertical, the weight is one of the other forces you have to account for.

    Collision from graphs

    Reading a collision off position–time graphs

    The graph shows the positions of two carts on a level track. Cart 1 (0.40 kg) rolls toward cart 2, which is at rest. Magnets on their bumpers push them apart during the shaded 0.20 s. Find (a) the mass of cart 2, (b) whether the collision is elastic, and (c) the average force each cart exerts on the other.

    Velocities are slopes. Take + as the way cart 1 starts, and read only the straight parts outside the shaded band:

    v1i=0.601.0=+0.60m/s v1f=0.20−0.403−2=−0.20m/s v2f=1.60−1.203−2=+0.40m/s

    (a) Momentum before = momentum after:

    (0.40)(0.60)=(0.40)(−0.20)+m2(0.40) 0.24=−0.08+0.40m2 m2=0.80kg

    (b) Kinetic energy before and after:

    Kbefore=12(0.40)(0.60)2=0.072J Kafter=12(0.40)(0.20)2+12(0.80)(0.40)2 Kafter=0.008+0.064=0.072J K is unchanged: elastic

    (c) Force on cart 1 = its change in momentum ÷ the contact time:

    F1=(0.40)(−0.20−0.60)0.20=−1.6N 1.6N on each cart, in opposite directions

    Cart 1 bounces back, so its slope after is negative. Drop that sign and m₂ comes out as 0.40 kg. Cart 2 gains +0.32 kg·m/s, exactly what cart 1 loses, so the forces on the two carts are equal and opposite (3rd law).

    External force on a system

    Two carts joined by a spring, pulled by a hand

    A 3.0 kg cart and a 1.0 kg cart are joined by a spring on a frictionless track, both at rest. A hand starts pulling the 1.0 kg cart with a steady 2.0 N, and the carts surge back and forth relative to each other as they go. (a) What is the acceleration of the center of mass? (b) How fast is the center of mass moving after 4.0 s? (c) At one instant the 1.0 kg cart's acceleration is 1.4 m/s². What is the 3.0 kg cart's acceleration then?

    System: both carts and the spring. The spring's pushes and pulls on the two carts are a 3rd-law pair inside the system, so they cancel. The only outside horizontal force is the hand:

    acm=FextMtotal=2.04.0 acm=0.50m/s2

    (b) The hand's impulse becomes the system's total momentum:

    FextΔt=Mtotalvcm (2.0)(4.0)=(4.0)vcm vcm=2.0m/s

    (c) Call the 1.0 kg cart A and the 3.0 kg cart B. At every instant their mass × acceleration must add up to the external force:

    mAaA+mBaB=Fext (1.0)(1.4)+(3.0)aB=2.0 aB=0.20m/s2

    Check with each cart's FBD: the spring pulls the 1.0 kg cart back with 2.0 − 1.4 = 0.60 N and the 3.0 kg cart forward with 0.60 N, and (3.0)(0.20) = 0.60 N.

    Each cart speeds up and slows down as the spring stretches and squashes, but the center of mass speeds up smoothly at 0.50 m/s², as if all 4.0 kg were one cart pulled by 2.0 N. Internal forces only pass momentum between the carts; only an external force changes the total.

    Bounce vs. stick, then a swing

    Rubber ball or clay ball: which swings the block higher?

    A 1.6 kg block hangs at rest from light strings. A 0.40 kg ball moving at 10 m/s hits it head-on. Case 1: the ball is clay and sticks. Case 2: the ball is rubber and bounces straight back at 2.0 m/s. How high does the block swing in each case?

    Two stages. During the hit, the system is ball + block and momentum is conserved. Take + toward the block.

    Case 1, clay (they move together):

    (0.40)(10)=(2.0)v→v=2.0m/s

    Case 2, rubber (the ball's velocity after is −2.0 m/s):

    (0.40)(10)=0.40(−2.0)+(1.6)vblock 4.0=−0.80+1.6vblock vblock=3.0m/s

    After the hit, the swing conserves energy (½mv² = mgh, so h = v²/2g):

    hclay=(2.0)22(10)=0.20m hrubber=(3.0)22(10)=0.45m clay 0.20 m; rubber 0.45 m

    The bouncing ball's momentum changes more (from +4.0 to −0.80 kg·m/s, a change of 4.8 instead of 3.2), and whatever momentum the ball loses, the block gains. So the rubber ball gives the block the bigger impulse and the higher swing, even though that bounce isn't elastic either (20 J before, 8.0 J after).

    Center of mass, outside forces

    A juggler's three balls

    A juggler keeps three 0.10 kg balls going, straight up and down. The pattern repeats every 0.50 s: for 0.30 s all three balls are in the air, then for 0.20 s one hand holds one ball (catching it and throwing it back up) while the other two fly. Take the three balls as the system. Find (a) the acceleration of their center of mass while all three are in the air, (b) the hand's average force over a whole cycle, (c) the hand's force while it holds a ball, and (d) the center of mass's acceleration then.

    (a) In the air, the only outside force on each ball is its weight:

    acm=g=10m/s2 down

    (b) The motion repeats, so the system's momentum is the same at the start and end of each cycle: the total impulse over a cycle is zero. Over the cycle the hand's upward impulse must cancel the total weight's downward impulse:

    Favg=3mg=3(0.10)(10) Favg=3.0N up

    (c) The hand only pushes for 0.20 s of each 0.50 s, but must deliver the same impulse:

    Fhand(0.20)=(3.0)(0.50) Fhand=7.5N up

    (d) While the hand pushes, the net outside force on the 0.30 kg system is 7.5 N up minus 3.0 N of weight:

    acm=7.5−3.00.30 acm=15m/s2 up

    Check: vcm drops (10)(0.30) = 3.0 m/s in the air and rises (15)(0.20) = 3.0 m/s in the hand, so it repeats. That's the sawtooth in the graph.

    Each ball does its own thing, but the system only cares about outside forces: weight all the time, plus the hand part of the time. A hand that pushes for 40% of the time has to push 1/0.40 = 2.5 times the balls' total weight.

    Three stages

    Spring launch, sticky hit, rough floor

    A spring (k = 400 N/m) fixed to a wall is squashed 0.10 m by a 1.0 kg block. Released, it launches the block across a frictionless floor into a 3.0 kg block at rest. The blocks stick, then slide onto a rough strip (μ = 0.25). How far do they slide on the strip?

    Stage 1, the launch (energy: spring energy becomes the 1.0 kg block's kinetic energy):

    12(400)(0.10)2=2.0J 2.0=12(1.0)v2→v=2.0m/s

    Stage 2, the hit (momentum; the blocks stick):

    (1.0)(2.0)=(4.0)vf→vf=0.50m/s

    Stage 3, the strip (friction's work removes the kinetic energy left after the hit):

    12(4.0)(0.50)2=μ(4.0)(10)d 0.50=(0.25)(40)d d=0.050m=5.0cm

    For the two-block system: in stage 1 the spring (pushing off the wall) is an outside force, so the momentum grows; in stage 2 momentum is conserved but 1.5 of the 2.0 J is lost; in stage 3 friction is outside and removes both. Skip stage 2 and set 2.0 J equal to friction's work, and you get 0.20 m, four times too far.

    Self-check

    Answer first, then open.

    1. A 7.0 kg bowling ball rolls at 2.0 m/s. A 0.060 kg tennis ball flies at 50 m/s. Which has more momentum?
      Answer
      Bowling ball: 14 kg·m/s. Tennis ball: 3.0 kg·m/s. The bowling ball has more than four times as much, even though it's much slower.
    2. An egg dropped onto a pillow survives; the same egg dropped onto the floor breaks. Both stop. Explain using impulse.
      Answer
      Both eggs have the same change in momentum, so the same impulse FΔt. The pillow makes the stopping time much longer, so the force on the egg is much smaller.
    3. Identical balls hit a wall at the same speed. One bounces straight back at the same speed; the other sticks to the wall. Which gets the bigger impulse from the wall?
      Answer
      The one that bounces. Its momentum changes from +mv to −mv, a change of 2mv. The one that sticks only changes by mv.
    4. A force on a 0.20 kg ball rises from 0 to 600 N and back to 0 over 0.010 s, in a triangle shape. If the ball started at rest, how fast is it moving afterward?
      Answer
      Impulse = triangle area = ½(0.010)(600) = 3.0 N·s. Δp = 3.0 kg·m/s, so v = 3.0/0.20 = 15 m/s.
    5. A cart moving at 3.0 m/s hits an identical cart at rest, and they stick. How fast do they move? What fraction of the kinetic energy is lost?
      Answer
      Momentum: m(3.0) = 2m vf, so vf = 1.5 m/s. K before: ½m(9) = 4.5m; K after: ½(2m)(2.25) = 2.25m. Half the kinetic energy is lost.
    6. A truck hits a fly. Which has the bigger change in momentum? The bigger acceleration?
      Answer
      Same size change in momentum: the forces are equal and opposite and act for the same time. The fly has a hugely bigger acceleration (and change in velocity), because its mass is tiny.
    7. A ball moving at 3.0 m/s hits an identical ball at rest head-on, and the collision is elastic. What happens?
      Answer
      The first ball stops and the second moves off at 3.0 m/s. That's the only result that keeps both momentum (3.0m) and kinetic energy (4.5m) the same, as in a Newton's cradle.
    8. An 80 kg astronaut floating in space throws a 2.0 kg wrench at 8.0 m/s. What happens to her?
      Answer
      She recoils the opposite way: (80)v = −(2.0)(8.0), so v = −0.20 m/s. Total momentum stays zero.
    9. A 3.0 kg cart moves at 4.0 m/s toward a 1.0 kg cart at rest on a frictionless track. What is the velocity of their center of mass before they collide? After?
      Answer
      vcm = (3.0 × 4.0 + 0)/(4.0) = 3.0 m/s, and it's still 3.0 m/s after the collision, whatever kind of collision it is. Only an outside force could change it.
    10. In a ballistic pendulum, why can't you set the bullet's kinetic energy equal to mgh of the swing?
      Answer
      The bullet sticks in the block: that collision is perfectly inelastic, and most of the kinetic energy turns into thermal energy and deforming the block. Momentum is conserved during the hit; energy is only conserved during the swing afterward.
    11. How can a rocket speed up in space, where there's nothing to push against?
      Answer
      It pushes its exhaust gas backward, and the gas pushes the rocket forward (3rd law). The backward momentum of the exhaust equals the forward momentum the rocket gains, so total momentum stays the same.
    12. Who's right? A steady 2.0 N force pushes a 1.0 kg cart and, separately, a 4.0 kg cart, each from rest across the same 1.0 m of frictionless track. Ana: “They end up with the same kinetic energy, but the 4.0 kg cart has more momentum.” Ben: “Same push, so the same momentum, and the faster 1.0 kg cart has more kinetic energy.”
      Answer
      Ana. Kinetic energy gained is force × distance: (2.0)(1.0) = 2.0 J for both. Momentum gained is force × time, and the heavy cart takes longer to cover the meter (2.0 s vs. 1.0 s), so it gets 4.0 kg·m/s to the light cart's 2.0. Ben's answer would be right if the force acted for the same time: then the momenta match, and the light cart gets more kinetic energy (K = p²/2m).
    13. A cart's momentum–time graph is a straight line from +6.0 kg·m/s to −4.0 kg·m/s over 0.50 s. What is the net force on it? What is the net force at the instant its momentum is zero?
      Answer
      The slope of p–t is the net force: (−4.0 − 6.0)/0.50 = −20 N, the same all the way through because the line is straight. At p = 0 the force is still −20 N: that's the instant the cart turns around, not a moment with no force.
    14. Who's right? A spring launcher on wheels, at rest on a frictionless floor, fires a ball forward. Maya: “The launcher pushes the ball and the ball pushes back just as hard, so their work cancels and the system's kinetic energy doesn't change.” Leo: “Those forces cancel in the momentum, which stays zero, but they don't cancel in the energy: the kinetic energy goes up.”
      Answer
      Leo. The two forces are equal and opposite and act for the same time, so their impulses cancel and the total momentum stays zero. But work is force × distance: the ball moves forward while pushed forward, and the launcher moves backward while pushed backward, so both forces do positive work. The kinetic energy comes out of the spring's stored energy, so the mechanical energy of ball + launcher + spring is constant; for ball + launcher alone, it increases.
    15. A toy cannon fires a marble at the same speed every time, and the cannon slides back across a rough floor before stopping. If weights double the cannon's mass, how does its slide distance change?
      Answer
      It slides ¼ as far. The marble carries off the same momentum, so the cannon recoils with the same momentum: twice the mass means half the speed. Friction slows it at μg whatever its mass, and stopping distance goes as v², so half the speed gives a quarter of the distance.
    16. Box A (0.60 kg) and box B (0.40 kg) are joined by a stretched spring, held one above the other and released. Their momentum–time graphs are straight lines with slopes −8.0 N for A and −2.0 N for B. What is the acceleration of the two-box system's center of mass, and how hard does the spring pull?
      Answer
      Net force on the system = sum of the slopes = −10 N, so acm = 10/1.0 = 10 m/s² down: just g, as you'd expect when weight is the only outside force (the spring's pulls cancel inside the system). Spring: A's weight is 6.0 N, so the spring pulls A down with 8.0 − 6.0 = 2.0 N; it pulls B up with 4.0 − 2.0 = 2.0 N.
    17. A 1.0 kg block and a 2.0 kg block, joined by a stretched spring, are released from rest on a frictionless floor and slide toward each other. Partway in, both cross rough strips (μ = 0.20) at the same time. What does the center of mass do before the strips? On them?
      Answer
      Before: it stays put. The spring's forces are internal and the total momentum stays zero. On the strips: friction on each block opposes its motion, 2.0 N on the light block and 4.0 N on the heavy one, in opposite directions. The net outside force is 2.0 N, pointing the way the light block is moving (against the heavy block's motion), so the center of mass starts to move that way at 2.0/3.0 = 0.67 m/s².
